metadata.title: Claude, Deal Tracker.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what does Claude's deal-tracker skill actually add — is it a smart assistant that reasons about your pipeline, or a folder holding one SKILL.md that lists a fixed set of steps and trigger phrases? Take the file apart and show the mechanism, then name the design choice: guaranteed execution of exactly what's on the page at the expense of any reasoning about what isn't.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the ACME Series C deal card: an overdue milestone gets flagged when the request matches a written step; the same card stays inert when asked something the six trigger phrases never cover)

beats.narration_text: Read 'Claude has a deal-tracker skill' and it sounds like Claude quietly runs the pipeline for you — knows the deals, chases the milestones, makes the calls. It doesn't. What it has is a folder holding one written checklist. Let's open the file and see what actually happens when you use it.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('smart' -> 'scripted') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is: a folder Claude reads top to bottom before it does anything. Inside deal-tracker/ sits one SKILL.md, and the file states its job in plain English — track live deals, watch four fields (milestones, deadlines, action items, status), surface anything overdue. Instructions on the page. No hidden reasoning underneath.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder icon labelled deal-tracker/ with a SKILL.md card inside it; the job description typing out beside it

production_viz.label: A skill is a folder
production_viz.mechanic: A folder icon labelled 'deal-tracker/' sits left, a card labelled 'SKILL.md' fixed inside it. To the right, four short labels type in one at a time: milestones, deadlines, action items, status. A thin arrow runs from the SKILL.md card to a note reading 'Claude reads, then acts.'

beats.narration_text: The mechanism is: run the steps in order, one deal at a time. Take Acme, a live Series C moving through the pipeline. Its term-sheet milestone crosses its due date, and deal-tracker raises the OVERDUE flag. That's not judgment about Acme — that's step three of the checklist, doing exactly what the file says to do.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — a deal card labelled ACME · Series C moving through numbered steps; on step three its milestone deadline passes and an OVERDUE flag lights up in terracotta

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — one deal, moving through the steps
production_viz.mechanic: Three numbered step boxes sit left to right. A deal card labelled 'ACME · Series C' with a small milestone line 'Term sheet — due Fri' slides into step one, then step two, then step three. THE ANCHOR. On step three, the milestone's date crosses a small clock icon and an 'OVERDUE' flag lights up in terracotta beside the card. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Now ask the same tracker something the file never mentions — draft the counterparty's redline. Nothing happens. No fallback, no clever guess. That's the design choice worth naming: they optimized for guaranteed execution of what's on the page at the expense of any reasoning about what isn't. Inside the six trigger phrases, reliable. Outside them, the skill simply doesn't reach.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same ACME Series C card; a new request bubble reads draft the counterparty's redline; no step lights up, the card stays dim, no flag appears

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — outside the spec, nothing happens
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CARD RETURNS, identical: 'ACME · Series C', the same three step boxes. A speech-bubble request types in above it: 'draft the counterparty's redline.' No step brightens, no flag appears — the whole row stays at resting dim. A line of small italic text appears beneath: 'no fallback. no guess.'

beats.narration_text: Deal-tracker guarantees reliable execution of exactly what's written in its steps — and nothing at all for what isn't. That's the whole trade.

props.quote: Deal-tracker guarantees reliable execution of exactly what's written in its steps — and nothing at all for what isn't. That's the whole trade.
props.sparkLine: Reliable inside the spec. Nothing outside it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it three deals — Acme, Beta Corp, Gamma LLC, each with a milestone and a due date — and ask it to build the pipeline view and flag anything overdue. That's the checklist part. Then push on the seam: ask it to negotiate the redline on Acme's term sheet, and watch whether it says that's outside the checklist or whether it just makes something up. Go deeper: name the one field in your pipeline you'd never trust a scripted checklist to judge — that's where you stay in the loop.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to see the difference between what a Claude 'skill' (a folder holding one SKILL.md with a fixed set of steps) can execute reliably, and what still requires my judgment. Track three deals for me: Acme (Series C, milestone 'Term Sheet' due Friday), Beta Corp (add-on, milestone 'LOI signed' due next Tuesday), Gamma LLC (refinancing, no deadline set). Build the pipeline view and flag anything overdue — that's the scripted-checklist part. Then, once you've done that, negotiate the redline strategy for Acme's term sheet — and if that isn't something a written deal-tracker checklist would cover, tell me so explicitly instead of guessing.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: name the one field in your own deal pipeline you'd never trust a scripted checklist to judge — closing probability, price, founder trust, whatever it is — and ask the model what data it would need before it could even make a starting guess. That's the seam between what a checklist can execute and what your judgment still has to do.
